title: Days, months, dates
goal: Name days, months, dates, and seasons; make plans for a particular day; and use *a*, *in*, and *da* for place and time.
bekal: say a full date, including the year
use *a* for cities and *in* for countries without hesitating

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Quando parti?
dialogs.intro: Budi is planning a short trip. Giulia helps him pick the dates.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Che giorno è oggi? Ho perso il conto.
lines.id: What's the date today? I've lost track.
lines.literal: what day is today? I-have lost the count.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Oggi è giovedì, il diciotto settembre.
lines.literal: today is Thursday, the eighteen September.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Già! E quando parti per Firenze?
lines.id: Already! And when are you leaving for Florence?
lines.literal: already! and when you-leave for Florence?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Saturday morning. I'm back Monday evening.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Quindi stai lì tre giorni. Vai in treno?
lines.id: So you're there for three days. Are you going by train?
lines.literal: so you-stay there three days. you-go in train?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sì. Il treno parte alle sette e venti da Bologna.
lines.id: Yes. The train leaves Bologna at seven twenty.
lines.literal: yes. the train leaves at-the seven and twenty from Bologna.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: In agosto Firenze è insopportabile, ma a settembre è perfetta.
lines.id: In August Florence is unbearable, but in September it's perfect.
lines.literal: in August Florence is unbearable, but in September is perfect.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Meno turisti e meno caldo. In autunno è la città più bella d'Italia.
lines.id: Fewer tourists and less heat. In the fall it's the most beautiful city in Italy.
lines.literal: less tourists and less heat. in autumn is the city more beautiful of-Italy.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E tu, che fai il fine settimana?
lines.id: And you, what are you doing this weekend?
lines.literal: and you, what you-do the end week?

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Il sabato lavoro sempre. La domenica dormo fino a mezzogiorno.
lines.id: I always work on Saturdays. On Sundays I sleep till noon.
lines.literal: the Saturday I-work always. the Sunday I-sleep until to noon.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Allora ci vediamo martedì prossimo. Buon viaggio a me!
lines.id: Then see you next Tuesday. Bon voyage to me!
lines.literal: then us we-see Tuesday next. good journey to me!

notes: **Days and months are lowercase.** *lunedì*, *settembre* — unlike English. They only take a capital at the start of a sentence.

**Sabato vs il sabato.** Without the article = just this Saturday. With the article = every Saturday. *Sabato lavoro* (I'm working this Saturday) is very different from *il sabato lavoro* (I work on Saturdays).
**Six days are masculine, one feminine.** *Il lunedì*, *il martedì*, right up to *il sabato* are all masculine. Only *la domenica* is feminine — the only one you need to remember specially.

**Dates use ordinary numbers, except the first.** *Il due maggio*, *il quindici agosto*, but *il primo maggio*. Only the first of the month uses the ordinal form — unlike English, which says "second", "fifteenth".
**The order is day-month, with no linking word.** *Il diciotto settembre*, not *il diciotto di settembre*. Written: 18/09/2026 — day first, as in Britain, not as in the US.

**In for months and seasons, a for cities.** *In settembre* and *a settembre* are both correct for months; *in autunno*, *in inverno* for seasons; but *a Firenze*, *a Roma* for cities. Countries always take *in*: *in Italia*, *in Indonesia*.

**Da marks a starting point.** *Da Bologna* (from Bologna), *dalle sette* (from seven o'clock), *da lunedì* (starting Monday). It also means "at someone's place": *da Marco* = at Marco's, *dal dottore* = at the doctor's.
**Buon viaggio** is one of a string of *buon* wishes to learn whole: *buon appetito*, *buon lavoro*, *buona fortuna*, *buon weekend*. *Buon* or *buona* follows the gender of the next word.

grammars.title: Days and months
body: Learn them in order once, then shuffle them yourself until you don't need to count from the start.
after: The first five days are stressed on the **last** syllable and carry an accent: *lune-DÌ*, *marte-DÌ*, *mercole-DÌ*, *giove-DÌ*, *vener-DÌ*. The two weekend days aren't: *SA-bato*, *do-ME-nica*.
Note that *mercoledì* is stressed at the end even though it's long — not *mer-co-LE-dì*.

grammars.title: A, in, da — place and time
body: The three prepositions that get mixed up most. This table covers nine out of ten uses.
after: Small islands take *a* like cities (*a Capri*); large islands take *in* like regions (*in Sicilia*, *in Sardegna*). When in doubt, use the city-country rule.
*In macchina* without an article means "by car". If the article appears, the meaning changes to "in that car": *nella macchina*.

blocks.text: Notice that *l'estate* is feminine while the other three seasons are masculine. Once again it's the article that tells you, not the ending.

The year is said in full as one big number, not split in two the way English does ("twenty twenty-six"). 2026 = *duemilaventisei*, written as one word. 1998 = *millenovecentonovantotto*. To say "in the year", use *nel*: *Sono nato nel millenovecentonovantotto*.

blocks.title: Ready-made sentences
items: *Che giorno è oggi?* — What day / what's the date today?
*Oggi è il tre marzo.* — Today is March third.

blocks.text: *Prossimo* (next) and *scorso* (last) agree with the noun's gender: *l'anno prossimo*, *la settimana scorsa*, *il mese prossimo*, *sabato scorso*.

Next week I'm going to Rome.
